unit.title: Salts
unit.blurb: What salts are, naming the salt made by an acid, and preparing salts from bases, carbonates and metals, including making copper sulfate crystals.

O1.t: Describe a salt as an ionic compound in which the hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal or ammonium ion, and give uses of salts.

O3.t: Write word equations for acids with metal carbonates and with metals.

O4.t: Describe and explain how to prepare a pure, dry sample of a soluble salt.

captions: Welcome to Atomic Education.
This lesson was written by the Atomic teaching team to
help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence.
Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 7: Salts.
Salt flavours our food, keeps our bodies working,
preserves food and even melts ice on winter roads.
It's made by mining, pumping water into underground salt beds, or evaporating seawater.
But table salt is just one of many salts!
Table salt, sodium chloride, is just one salt.
Ammonium nitrate is used in fertilisers,
calcium sulfate in plaster casts for broken bones,
and sodium hydrogen carbonate is baking soda.
A salt is an ionic compound.
Sodium chloride is made of positive sodium ions and negative chloride ions.
Every acid contains hydrogen ions,
and a salt forms when those hydrogen ions
are replaced by metal ions or ammonium ions.
A common way to make a salt is to react an acid with a base:
acid plus base gives salt plus water.
Common acids are hydrochloric, sulfuric and nitric acid.
Bases are metal oxides and metal hydroxides.
Bases that dissolve in water are called alkalis, like sodium hydroxide; others,
like copper oxide, are insoluble but still react with acids.
Hydrochloric acid plus potassium hydroxide gives potassium chloride and water.
The metal comes from the base, the rest from the acid:
hydrochloric acid makes chlorides, sulfuric makes sulfates, nitric makes nitrates.
Hydrochloric acid is neutralised exactly with sodium hydroxide solution: the indicator shows green,
pH 7. The solution is then heated gently in an evaporating dish.
Predict: what will be left in the dish?
Pause and decide.
Watch. As the solution is heated, the water evaporates.
Small white crystals are left in the dish.
They are sodium chloride: table salt.
Explain what you saw.
The acid and the alkali reacted to make a salt and water:
hydrochloric acid plus sodium hydroxide gives sodium chloride plus water.
The water evaporated, leaving the salt as crystals.
The sodium came from the alkali,
and the chloride came from the hydrochloric acid.
Pause and explain it in your own words.

captions: Magnesium ribbon is added to dilute hydrochloric acid in one tube,
and marble chips, calcium carbonate, to the acid in another.
Both fizz. Predict: is the same gas made in both tubes?
Pause and decide.
Watch. A lit splint held at the mouth of
the magnesium tube goes out with a squeaky pop.
The gas from the marble chips is bubbled through limewater, which turns milky.
Explain what you saw.
The gases are different.
Acid plus metal gives a salt plus hydrogen,
which burns with a squeaky pop.
Acid plus a metal carbonate gives a salt, water and carbon dioxide,
which turns limewater milky.
Both tubes make a salt: magnesium chloride and calcium chloride.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
Salts can also be made from metal carbonates.
Drop a seashell, made of calcium carbonate, into vinegar and it fizzes.
Acid plus metal carbonate gives salt, carbon dioxide and water.
Sulfuric acid and copper carbonate make copper sulfate.
Acid plus metal gives salt plus hydrogen:
hydrochloric acid and zinc make zinc chloride.
We use magnesium, iron or zinc, because copper, silver and gold don't react,
and sodium and potassium are too violent.
To prepare copper sulfate, warm dilute sulfuric acid gently,
then add copper carbonate a little at a time, stirring,
until some is left over and no longer reacts.
Adding excess makes sure all the acid is used up.
Filter the mixture to remove the unreacted copper carbonate.
Collect the blue filtrate,
then heat it gently in an evaporating dish to remove most of the water,
making a saturated solution.
Leave the saturated solution to cool, and blue copper sulfate crystals form.
Filter them and dry them on filter paper.
The same method makes zinc chloride from zinc and hydrochloric acid.
Now it is your turn to shine!
Pause the video after each question and try to answer it first.
Question 1: Complete: acid + base gives...
Pause the video now.
Answer: Salt and water.
Question 2: Which gas is given off when an acid reacts with a metal carbonate?
Pause the video now.
Answer: Carbon dioxide.
Question 3: Name the salt made from sulfuric acid and magnesium.
Pause the video now.
Answer: Magnesium sulfate.
Question 4: Why is excess metal carbonate added when making a salt?
Pause the video now.
Answer: To make sure all the acid reacts.
